mainTopic: Direct force (כֹּחוֹ) versus indirect causing (גרמא): when someone who causes a death is חייב or פטור
overview: This amud is about when a person who causes a death counts as the killer, and when it is only indirect causing (גרמא). It opens by finishing the case of turning a vat over someone: under a vat the stifling air starts right away, so it differs from the marble house. Next, a סימן lists four rulings of רבא. In the ladder, shield and herbs cases the attacker is פטור, because at the moment he acted the victim could still escape, be protected, or be healed. רב אשי adds that herbs in the market, or herbs that came by chance, also exempt the shooter. In the fourth case, a stone that bounces off a wall and kills, the thrower is חייב. A ברייתא about ball players supports this, and another ברייתא adds a four-אמות distance rule. The גמרא then defends the idea that a forceful rebound is still the thrower's own force (כֹּחוֹ) against two contradictions from משניות in פרה. Finally, רב פפא rules on killing with a stream of water and on a stone thrown up that veers sideways. מר בר רב אשי's challenge to the sideways ruling continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why the vat case is different from the marble house
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes distinguishing the two cases. In the marble house, the deadly heat does not begin right away without a lamp. Under a vat, the stifling air begins right away even without a lamp.
steps.simpleTranslation: [There, without a lamp, the heat does not start] at the time of the act. Here, under the vat, even without a lamp the stifling heat starts at the time of the act.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an argument that two cases cannot be compared. Closing someone in a marble house is different from turning a vat over him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the marble house, the room is big enough to breathe in, so only the lit lamp makes the air deadly. Under a vat, the air starts choking him the moment the vat comes down, lamp or no lamp. Because the timing of the danger is different, a ruling about one case cannot be used as a proof about the other.

keyTerms.meaning: At its time: right when the act is done
Here: the case we are discussing now (the vat)
Heat or stifling air that causes suffocation

steps.confusionAlert: This step begins in the middle of a sentence. The first word finishes the line about the marble house: 'there, without a lamp, the heat does not start right away.'

phrases.english: at that time.
Here, even without a lamp,
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the case of turning a vat over someone.

phrases.english: the stifling heat begins at that time.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא, בְּלָא שְׁרָגָא נָמֵי מַתְחֵיל הַבְלָא בְּשַׁעְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a distinction begun in the previous section of the daf (the marble house versus the vat).
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects comparing the marble-house ruling to the vat case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The two cases differ in when the danger begins. In the marble house it begins only once the lamp is lit; under a vat it begins immediately.

steps.title: A memory aid for the coming rulings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a סימן (memory aid) listing key words from the rulings that follow: ladder, shield, herbs, in a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: (Memory aid: ladder, shield, herbs, in a wall.)
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא gives a short list of words to help you remember the order of the rulings it is about to bring.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word points to one of רבא's rulings that follow. 'Ladder' is the pit case (step 3), 'shield' is the arrow case (step 4), 'herbs' is the healing-herbs case (step 5), and 'in a wall' is the stone that bounces off a wall (step 9).

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid listing key words of the coming teachings

phrases.english: (Mnemonic: ladder, shield,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the words in round brackets and some don't. They're just a memory aid, not a ruling.

phrases.english: herbs, in a wall).

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: None, this is a structural marker
steps.triggerLanguage: סִימָן: סוּלָּם, תְּרִיס, סַמָּנִין, בַּכּוֹתֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the vat discussion to a new series of rulings by רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling. This only organizes the teachings that follow.

steps.title: Pushed into a pit that had a ladder
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if someone pushed a person into a pit that had a ladder, and the ladder was then removed, the pusher is פטור. This is true even if the pusher himself removed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If someone pushed a person into a pit, and there was a ladder in the pit, and someone else came and took it away, or even if the pusher himself hurried and took it away, he is exempt. At the moment he threw him in, the victim could still climb out.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a ruling: pushing someone into a pit that has a ladder does not make you liable for his death, even if the ladder is removed later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What counts is the moment of the push. At that moment the victim could still climb out, so the push itself was not deadly. Taking the ladder away only stops him from being saved. That is indirect, so the pusher is פטור from execution, even if he removed the ladder himself.
steps.confusionAlert: פטור here means he is not executed by בית דין. It does not mean he did nothing wrong.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the key rule: liability for killing is judged by whether the act was deadly at the moment it was done.

phrases.english: Rava said: If one pushed him into a pit,
and there was a ladder in the pit,
and another person came and removed it,
and even if he himself hurried and removed it, he is exempt,
phrases.notes: 'He himself' means the person who did the pushing.

phrases.english: because at the time that he threw him in,
he was able to climb out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: דְּחָפוֹ לְבוֹר, וְסוּלָּם בַּבּוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The first case in the memory aid ('ladder').
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the victim could still escape at the moment of the push, the pusher is פטור, even if he later removed the means of escape himself.

steps.title: Shooting an arrow at someone holding a shield
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if someone shot an arrow at a person holding a shield, and the shield was then taken away, the shooter is פטור. This is true even if the shooter took it himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: If someone shot an arrow, and the victim had a shield in his hand, and someone else came and took it, or even if the shooter himself hurried and took it, he is exempt. At the moment he shot at him, his arrows were blocked.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second ruling built on the same idea. Shooting at a person protected by a shield does not make you liable for his death, even if the shield is removed before the arrow hits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the moment the arrow was shot, the shield would have stopped it, so the shot itself was not deadly. The death came about only because the shield was removed afterward, which is indirect. Like the ladder case, the timing of the act decides liability.
steps.whatToRemember: In רבא's ladder and shield cases, and in the herbs case in step 5, the attacker is פטור because at the moment he acted, the victim was still protected or could still be saved. Removing that protection afterward makes the killing indirect, even when the attacker removes it himself.

phrases.english: And Rava said: If one shot an arrow,
and there was a shield in his hand,
and another person came and took it,
and even if he himself hurried and took it, he is exempt,
because at the time that he shot at him,
his arrows were blocked.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: זָרַק חֵץ, וּתְרִיס בְּיָדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second case in the memory aid ('shield'), resting on the same reasoning as the ladder case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the victim was protected at the moment the arrow was shot, the shooter is פטור, even if he later took the shield away himself.

steps.title: Shooting an arrow when the victim had healing herbs
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if the victim had herbs that could heal the arrow wound, the shooter is פטור, even if the herbs were later scattered by someone else or by the shooter himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If someone shot an arrow at a person who had healing herbs in his hand, and someone else came and scattered the herbs, or even if the shooter himself rushed to scatter them, the shooter is exempt. The reason is that at the moment he shot, the victim could still have been healed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the third ruling from the סימן, the 'herbs' case. The shooter is not put to death because, when he shot, the wound was curable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same pattern as the ladder and shield cases. The court judges the shooter by the situation at the moment of the act. At that moment the herbs were there, so the arrow alone was not a deadly act. The death came from the herbs being taken away afterward.

phrases.english: And Rava said: If one shot an arrow at him,
and he had healing herbs in his hand,
and another person came and scattered them,
and even if he himself rushed and scattered them, he is exempt,
because at the time that he shot at him
he was able to be healed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: זָרַק בּוֹ חֵץ, וְסַמָּנִין בְּיָדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The third case in the list from the סימן, built the same way as the ladder and shield rulings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the wound could be healed at the time of shooting, the shooter is exempt, even if he himself later removed the cure.

steps.title: Even herbs available in the market
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי concludes from רבא's reasoning that even if the herbs were only available in the market, the shooter is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Therefore, even if the healing herbs were available in the market, the shooter is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי takes רבא's reasoning one step further. The herbs do not have to be in the victim's hand. If they can be bought in the market, that is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's reason was that the victim 'could be healed' at the time of the shooting. If herbs are for sale in the market, the victim could still be healed. So the same reason exempts the shooter here too.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: Therefore,
even if the herbs are in the market, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: הִלְכָּךְ, אֲפִילּוּ סַמָּנִין בַּשּׁוּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a wider rule from רבא's reason in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If herbs can be bought in the market, the wound counts as curable and the shooter is exempt.

steps.title: What if herbs just happened to come to him
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרבא asks רב אשי about a victim to whom herbs came only by chance.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא the son of רבא asked רב אשי: If herbs happened to come into his hands, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A question is asked about a weaker case. The herbs were not in his hand or in the market. They just happened to reach him. This step sets up רב אשי's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the market case, herbs were normally available. Here they were not normally available and only showed up by chance. The question is whether such a chance cure still makes the wound count as 'curable'.

keyTerms.meaning: Happened to come / became available by chance

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha, son of Rava, said to Rav Ashi:
If herbs happened to come to him, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: נִזְדַּמְּנוּ לוֹ סַמָּנִין, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests how far רב אשי's widening in step 6 goes.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a cure that came only by chance still exempt the shooter?

steps.title: He left court innocent
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that in this case too the shooter is exempt. He has 'left court innocent'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He has already gone out of court innocent.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the question. Even herbs that came by chance make the shooter exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the victim actually had a cure available, the arrow did not certainly cause the death. So the shooter cannot be executed as a murderer.
steps.whatToRemember: A shooter is exempt whenever the victim had a real way to be healed: herbs in his hand, herbs in the market, or herbs that came to him by chance.

phrases.english: He said to him:
He has already gone out of court innocent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הֲרֵי יָצָא מִבֵּית דִּין זַכַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא's question from step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Herbs that came by chance also make the shooter exempt.

steps.title: A stone that bounces off a wall and kills
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if someone throws a stone at a wall and it bounces back and kills, the thrower is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: If someone threw a stone at a wall, and it bounced back and killed someone, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the last ruling from the סימן, the 'in a wall' case. This time the thrower is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here, unlike the earlier cases, nothing new stepped in after the throw. The bounce comes directly from the force of the throw itself. So the killing is counted as the thrower's own act.

phrases.english: And Rava said: If one threw a stone at a wall,
and it bounced back and killed, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: זָרַק צְרוֹר בַּכּוֹתֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The final case of the סימן. Unlike the earlier cases, this one ends in liability.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A killing by a stone bouncing back from a wall is counted as the thrower's act, so he is liable.

steps.title: A ברייתא about ball players supports רבא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that ball players who kill with a bouncing ball are executed if it was intentional and exiled if it was accidental.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a תנא taught the same thing: For example, people playing with a ball who killed someone. If it was on purpose, they are executed. If it was by accident, they go into exile.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that matches רבא's ruling. A ball that bounces off a wall and kills is treated like a direct killing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ball players throw the ball against a wall so it comes back. The ברייתא gives them the full penalties for killing. This shows that a deadly bounce off a wall counts as the thrower's act, just as רבא said.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Our תנא also taught it': a source that supports the ruling
They go into exile (to a city of refuge)

phrases.english: And our tanna also taught it:
For example, those who play with a ball who killed someone,
if on purpose, they are executed;
if by accident, they go into exile.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנָּא תּוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רבא's ruling in step 9 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's ruling that a bounced stone makes the thrower liable.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about ball players who kill with a bouncing ball.

steps.title: Why say the accidental killers go to exile?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needed to say that accidental ball-player killers go into exile, since that seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'By accident they go into exile.' That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the ברייתא. It asks why it bothered to state something obvious. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Anyone who kills by accident goes into exile. So the accidental part of the ברייתא seems to teach nothing new. The גמרא wants to know what new lesson the ברייתא is really teaching.

phrases.english: 'By accident they go into exile' — that is obvious!

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּשׁוֹגֵג גּוֹלִין, פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא brought in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The accidental part of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: All accidental killers go into exile, so stating it here seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The real lesson: intentional players are executed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the new lesson is the intentional part. We might have thought the warning was too uncertain, since nobody knows if the ball will bounce back.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed for 'on purpose, they are executed.' You might have said: this is an uncertain warning, because who can say the ball will bounce back? So it teaches us that they are executed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The ברייתא's real point is that someone who kills on purpose with a bouncing ball can be executed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To execute someone, he must be warned (התראה) before the act. We might think the warning here is a התראת ספק, because no one can be sure the ball will come back. The ברייתא teaches that it still counts as a full warning, so the killer can be executed.

keyTerms.meaning: An uncertain warning, when it is not sure the act will lead to the punishment

steps.whatToRemember: A stone or ball that bounces off a wall and kills counts as the thrower's own act. On purpose, he is executed. By accident, he goes into exile.
steps.confusionAlert: The new lesson is NOT the exile part. It is that the intentional killer can be executed, even though we might have thought the warning was uncertain.

phrases.english: 'On purpose, they are executed' is what he needed to teach.
You might have said:
it is an uncertain warning,
phrases.notes: The killer must be warned before the act to be executed. Here, no one knows for sure the act will kill.

phrases.english: who can say that it will bounce back?
So it teaches us that they are executed.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמֵזִיד נֶהֱרָגִין אִיצְטְרִיךְ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 11 by moving the new lesson to the intentional part.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the new lesson to a different clause of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A warning about a bouncing ball is an uncertain warning, so the killer cannot be executed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The warning counts, and the intentional killer is executed.

steps.title: Ball players: within four cubits exempt, beyond four cubits liable
steps.stepSummary: רב תחליפא teaches a ברייתא before רבי אבהו. Ball players who kill are פטור within four אמות and חייב beyond four אמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב תחליפא from the West taught before רבי אבהו: ball players who killed someone are exempt if it was within four cubits, and liable if it was beyond four cubits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא about ball players who kill. This one adds a distance rule of four אמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier ברייתא said accidental ball-player killers go to גלות. This ברייתא sets a limit: below four אמות they are פטור. Above four אמות they are חייב.

keyTerms.meaning: Four cubits, a common measure of distance

phrases.english: Rav Tachlifa from the West taught
phrases.notes: 'The West' means ארץ ישראל, which is west of בבל.

phrases.english: before Rabbi Abbahu:
for example, those who play with a ball and killed someone,
within four cubits, he is exempt,
beyond four cubits, he is liable.
phrases.notes: Liable here means he goes to גלות, since this is talking about an accident.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי רַב תַּחְלִיפָא בַּר מַעְרְבָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a distance condition to the ball-player law from the earlier ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ball player who kills is פטור within four אמות and חייב beyond four אמות.

steps.title: Why should distance matter?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רב אשי why four אמות should make a difference. Either the thrower wanted the result or he didn't.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: What is the case? If he is happy with it, he should be liable even for a little distance. If he is not happy with it, he should not be liable even for a lot.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges the four-אמות rule. He says the distance itself should not decide anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liability should depend on whether the thrower wanted the ball to go where it went. If he wanted a short bounce, he should be חייב even under four אמות. If he did not want it, he should be פטור even beyond four אמות. So why use a fixed number?

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What case are we talking about?
He is pleased with it / he wants it

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
What are the circumstances?
If he is pleased with it,
then even a little distance should also make him liable.
If he is not pleased with it,
then even a lot of distance should not make him liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: הֵיכִי דָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the four-אמות line drawn in Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The four-אמות distinction in רב תחליפא's ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Liability should depend on whether the thrower wanted the result, not on a fixed distance.

steps.title: Ball players want the ball to come back far
steps.stepSummary: Ordinary ball players want the ball to bounce back far. So a long rebound is what they wanted, and a short one is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Ordinary ball players: the farther the ball goes, the happier they are.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers רבינא. The four-אמות line follows what ball players normally want.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We assume a normal player wants a long, strong rebound. So a rebound beyond four אמות matches his wish, and he is חייב. A short rebound under four אמות is not what he wanted, so he is פטור. The number fits what players usually intend.

phrases.english: He said to him: ordinary people who play with a ball,
the farther in they go,
phrases.notes: The closer the players get to the wall, the farther the ball bounces back, and that's what they want.

phrases.english: the more pleased they are.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: סְתָם מְשַׂחֲקִין בְּכַדּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the normal intention of the players
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The four אמות seemed random, with no link to what the thrower wanted.
steps.terutzMaskana: Ball players normally want a long rebound, so beyond four אמות counts as wanted and under four אמות does not.
steps.whatToRemember: Four אמות is not a random number. It reflects that ball players want the ball to bounce back far.

steps.title: Is a bounce really the thrower's force? A contradiction from פרה אדומה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a rebound counts as the thrower's own force. It points to a משנה in פרה: ashes that land on the hand or side first are פסול.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that in such a case it counts as his force? But a משנה contradicts this: if someone was mixing the ashes and the ashes fell on his hand or on the side, and only then fell into the trough, it is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the basic idea that a bounced ball is still the thrower's doing. It brings a contradicting משנה about mixing the ashes of the פרה אדומה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These ball-player rulings assume that a rebound off a wall still counts as the person's force (כֹּחוֹ). With the פרה אדומה ashes, though, if they hit something on the way into the water, it no longer counts as his act. Then a bounce off a wall should not count as his act either.

keyTerms.meaning: His force, meaning something done directly by his own action
And they pointed out a contradiction
Here: the ashes of the פרה אדומה put into water

phrases.english: Is this to say that in a case like this it is his force?
phrases.notes: 'A case like this' means the ball bouncing off the wall before hitting someone.

phrases.english: But they raised a contradiction:
One who sanctifies, and the sanctifying ashes fell
on his hand or on the side,
and afterward fell into the trough,
it is invalid.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דִּכְהַאי גַּוְונָא כֹּחוֹ הוּא? וּרְמִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the distance question to the basic question of whether a bounce counts as the thrower's force.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption (from רבא and the ברייתות) that a rebound counts as the thrower's force
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In פרה אדומה, ashes that hit something on the way do not count as the person's act. So a rebound off a wall should not count either.
steps.confusionAlert: The משנה is not about killing at all. The גמרא brings it only to learn whether something that bounces or stops on the way still counts as 'his force'.

steps.title: The ashes only trickled down
steps.stepSummary: The משנה in פרה is talking about ashes that trickled slowly into the water, without force. That is different from a ball flying hard off a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? With ashes that trickled down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction. In the פרה אדומה case, the ashes slid down slowly by themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ashes that slowly drip from the hand or the side into the water lost the person's push. They fell on their own, so it is not כֹּחוֹ. A ball that bounces off a wall is still moving from the thrower's strong throw, so it does count as his force.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
With ashes that trickle down.
phrases.notes: The ashes slid down slowly on their own, not pushed by his force.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן? בְּשׁוֹתֵת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction from פרה by limiting the משנה to a specific case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the contradicting source to a narrow case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Anything that bounces or stops on the way stops counting as the person's force.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a slow trickle loses the person's force. A forceful rebound off a wall is still כֹּחוֹ.
steps.whatToRemember: A ball bouncing hard off a wall is still the thrower's force. Ashes slowly trickling into water are not.
steps.whyThisMatters: This keeps רבא's rule (Step 9) and the ball-player rulings standing: a forceful rebound still counts as the thrower's act.

steps.title: A challenge from the needle on the shard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה in פרה. If it is unclear whether the water was sprinkled straight onto the needle, or onto the shard and then sprayed onto the needle, the sprinkling is פסול. This suggests that water bouncing off something does not count as the sprinkler's own force.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a needle was lying on a piece of pottery, and someone sprinkled. It is unclear whether he sprinkled on the needle, or sprinkled on the pottery and the water sprayed onto the needle. His sprinkling is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to attack the answer from step 17. Here the water hit the shard and then sprayed onto the needle with some force, yet it still does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 17 the גמרא said that slow trickling is different from a forceful rebound. But spraying off a shard sounds like a real rebound, and the sprinkling is still פסול. If so, a rebound would not count as the person's force. That is a problem for רבא's ruling about a stone bouncing off a wall (step 9) and for the ball-player rulings (steps 10-15).

keyTerms.meaning: It sprayed or squeezed off onto something

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A needle that was placed on a piece of pottery,
and someone sprinkled on it —
it is uncertain whether he sprinkled on the needle,
or whether he sprinkled on the pottery
and it sprayed onto it —
phrases.notes: 'It' here is the needle: the water bounced off the pottery onto the needle.

phrases.english: his sprinkling is invalid.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 17 that a forceful rebound counts as the person's force.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 17's claim that a forceful rebound, unlike slow trickling, counts as one's own force.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Water that sprays off a shard is a forceful rebound, yet the sprinkling is פסול. So a rebound should not count as one's own force.

steps.title: The משנה says 'found', not 'sprayed'
steps.stepSummary: רב חיננא בר יהודה, in the name of רב, says the correct wording of the משנה is 'found' (מצא), not 'sprayed' (מיצה). So the case is water simply found on the needle, with no forceful bounce.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חיננא בר יהודה said in the name of רב: the word that was taught is 'found'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by fixing the wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה says 'found', the case is that water was later found on the needle. Nobody knows whether it was sprinkled there or just dripped over from the shard. Dripping has no force, so the משנה tells us nothing about a forceful rebound, and the answer of step 17 still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: He found (water was found on the needle)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִינָּנָא בַּר יְהוּדָה מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: Rav Chinnana bar Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
"Found" is what was stated.
phrases.notes: Read מָצָא (found) instead of מִיצָּה (sprayed). The two words look almost the same.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִינָּנָא בַּר יְהוּדָה מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב: מָצָא אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18 by correcting the wording of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the wording of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה describes water spraying forcefully off the shard, so a rebound would not count as one's force.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה describes water found on the needle, with no forceful rebound, so it does not contradict step 17.
steps.whatToRemember: A forceful rebound can still count as the person's own force. The needle משנה was only about water found there, not water that bounced.

steps.title: Tying someone up and sending water onto him
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that if someone ties up another person and sends a stream of water onto him, the water is like his own arrows and he is חייב. This applies only to the first force of the water. The second force is just גרמא (indirect causing).
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: someone who ties up his friend and directs a stream of water onto him, it is like his own arrows, and he is liable. This is only with the first force. With the second force, it is merely indirect causing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from רב פפא about killing with water, which continues the theme of what counts as a person's own force.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the water rushes straight from his action onto the tied-up man, it is like shooting an arrow, so he is a killer. If the water first flows along and only later reaches the man on its own, it is just גרמא, and he is not חייב for רציחה.

keyTerms.meaning: A channel or stream of water
His own arrows; counts as his direct act
First force, coming straight from his action
Second force, after the water continues on its own
Indirect causing, not a direct act

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Someone who tied up his fellow,
and directed a stream of water onto him —
it is his own arrows,
phrases.notes: He means the water counts like a weapon the man shot himself.

phrases.english: and he is liable.
This applies only with the first force,
but with the second force —
it is merely indirect causing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: הַאי מַאן דְּכַפְתֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ball and needle discussion to a new ruling by רב פפא on direct and indirect force.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sending water onto a tied-up person is like shooting arrows, and he is חייב, but only with the first force. The second force is גרמא.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a clear line between a person's direct force, which makes him a killer, and גרמא, which does not.

steps.title: A stone thrown up that goes sideways
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that if someone throws a stone upward and it goes off to the side and kills someone, he is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב פפא said: if someone threw a stone upward and it went to the side and killed someone, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a second ruling about force. A stone that went in a different direction from where it was thrown still makes the thrower חייב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stone did not go where he aimed it, upward, but it still killed. רב פפא holds the thrower responsible anyway. The next step asks why.

phrases.english: And Rav Pappa said:
If one threw a stone upward
and it went to the side and killed — he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: זָרַק צְרוֹר לְמַעְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ruling by רב פפא on the same theme of a person's force.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who throws a stone upward and it veers sideways and kills is חייב.

steps.title: If it was his force, it should have gone up
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי challenges רב פפא: if the thrower is חייב because it was his force, then the stone should have gone upward, where he threw it, not to the side.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי said to רב פפא: What is the reason? Because it is his force? If it is his force, it should go up!
steps.whatsHappening: מר בר רב אשי questions the reason behind רב פפא's ruling in step 21. The challenge continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only reason to make the thrower חייב would be that his force killed. But his force sent the stone upward. Going sideways seems to come from something else, so why should it count as his force?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב פָּפָּא:
phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi said to Rav Pappa:
What is the reason?
Because it is his force?
If it is his force, it should go upward!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב פָּפָּא: מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning behind רב פפא's ruling in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's ruling that the thrower is חייב when the stone veers sideways.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His force pushed the stone upward. The sideways movement is not in the direction of his force, so it should not count as his act.
